items.title: Runnable, Callable & Thread
items.context: Runnable defines run() with no return value. Callable defines call(), which can return a value and throw checked exceptions — used with ExecutorService. Thread is the class representing an actual thread; implementing Runnable is generally preferred over extending Thread since it leaves you free to extend another class.

questions.prompt: Which interface's task method can return a value and throw a checked exception?
choices: Thread
Executor
Callable
Runnable
questions.explanation: Callable<V>.call() returns a V and is allowed to throw checked exceptions, unlike Runnable.run(). It's used with ExecutorService.submit().

questions.prompt: You want a class to define a background task but it already extends another class. What's your best option?
choices: Implement Runnable — Java doesn't allow extending two classes
Make every method synchronized
Extend Thread anyway, Java allows multiple inheritance
Use a static main method instead
questions.explanation: Since Java has no multiple inheritance of classes, implementing Runnable (an interface) keeps the class free to extend whatever it already extends.

items.title: Thread Pools & ExecutorService
items.context: Creating a new Thread per task is expensive and unbounded. A thread pool (via ExecutorService, typically obtained from Executors) reuses a fixed set of worker threads, queuing tasks when all workers are busy — better throughput and resource control.

questions.prompt: Why prefer a thread pool over creating a new Thread for every task?
choices: Java forbids creating threads directly
It removes the need for synchronization entirely
It reuses a bounded set of threads, avoiding the overhead and resource exhaustion of unbounded thread creation
Threads created manually run faster
questions.explanation: Thread creation/teardown is costly, and unbounded threads can exhaust memory/CPU; a pool caps concurrency and reuses worker threads across many tasks.

questions.prompt: Which class is the standard factory for obtaining common thread pool configurations in Java?
choices: Thread
ThreadGroup
Executors
Runnable
questions.explanation: Executors provides factory methods like newFixedThreadPool() and newCachedThreadPool() that return an ExecutorService.

items.title: Thread states
items.context: A thread moves through states: New (created, not started), Runnable (ready/running), Blocked/Waiting (waiting for a lock or another thread), Timed Waiting (waiting with a timeout), and Terminated (finished).

questions.prompt: A thread that has finished executing its run() method is in which state?
choices: New
Blocked
Terminated
Runnable
questions.explanation: Once run() completes (normally or via an uncaught exception), the thread enters the Terminated state permanently.

items.title: synchronized and volatile
items.context: synchronized ensures only one thread executes a block/method on a given lock at a time, preventing race conditions. volatile guarantees visibility — reads/writes always go to main memory rather than a thread-local cache — but it does NOT make compound operations like i++ atomic.

questions.prompt: Two threads call the same synchronized instance method on the same object at nearly the same time. What happens?
choices: One thread acquires the object's lock and runs to completion while the other waits
Both run simultaneously, results may be corrupted
The JVM throws a ConcurrentModificationException
Only the first thread's call is executed; the second is silently dropped
questions.explanation: synchronized methods/blocks acquire the object's intrinsic lock; a second thread trying to enter a synchronized section on the same lock blocks until the first one releases it.

questions.prompt: Does declaring a counter `volatile` make `counter++` thread-safe?
choices: No, volatile has no effect on multithreading
Yes, but only for int and long
Yes, volatile makes all operations on it atomic
No — volatile only guarantees visibility, not atomicity of compound operations like increment
questions.explanation: counter++ is really read-modify-write. volatile ensures every thread sees the latest value, but two threads can still race between the read and the write — use AtomicInteger or synchronization instead.

items.title: wait, notify, notifyAll
items.context: wait() releases the object's lock and pauses the current thread until notified. notify() wakes one waiting thread; notifyAll() wakes all of them. All three must be called from within a synchronized block/method on that same object — used classically in producer-consumer coordination.

questions.prompt: Which method wakes every thread currently waiting on an object's monitor?
choices: wait()
notifyAll()
interrupt()
notify()
questions.explanation: notify() wakes only one arbitrary waiting thread; notifyAll() wakes them all, letting each re-check its wait condition.

questions.prompt: Where must wait()/notify() calls appear for the code to even compile-run correctly?
choices: Inside a try-with-resources block
Anywhere in the class
Inside a synchronized block or method holding that object's lock
Only inside a static method
questions.explanation: wait()/notify()/notifyAll() throw IllegalMonitorStateException if the calling thread doesn't currently hold the lock on that object — they must be inside a synchronized context on it.

items.title: CountDownLatch
items.context: CountDownLatch lets one or more threads wait until a set of operations happening in other threads completes. It's initialized with a count; each countDown() call decrements it, and await() blocks until the count reaches zero.

questions.prompt: What is CountDownLatch used for?
choices: Limiting the number of threads in a pool
Preventing two threads from ever running at the same time
Automatically restarting failed threads
Letting one or more threads wait until a fixed number of other operations have completed
questions.explanation: A CountDownLatch starts at a fixed count; other threads call countDown() as they finish work, and any thread calling await() blocks until that count reaches zero — a one-time synchronization gate.

items.title: Atomic variables
items.context: Classes like AtomicInteger and AtomicLong provide lock-free, thread-safe operations (get, set, incrementAndGet, compareAndSet) built on low-level compare-and-swap (CAS) hardware instructions, avoiding the overhead of synchronized for simple counters.

questions.prompt: What does AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() provide that a plain `int` field's `count++` does not under concurrent access?
choices: Guaranteed ordering of unrelated variables
Faster single-threaded performance
Automatic persistence to disk
An atomic read-modify-write, so concurrent increments are never lost
questions.explanation: count++ is a non-atomic read-modify-write; two threads can race and lose an update. AtomicInteger's methods perform the whole operation atomically, typically via a CAS loop, with no lost updates.

questions.prompt: What technique do atomic classes typically rely on internally to update a value without locks?
choices: Thread.sleep() polling
Serializing the value to disk
synchronized blocks
Compare-and-swap (CAS)
questions.explanation: Atomic classes use compare-and-swap: read the current value, compute the new one, then atomically write it back only if the value hasn't changed since — retrying if it has.

items.title: Deadlock
items.context: A deadlock occurs when two or more threads are each waiting for a lock the other holds, so none can ever proceed. A common prevention strategy is always acquiring multiple locks in the same, consistent order across all threads.

questions.prompt: What is a deadlock?
choices: A thread that throws an uncaught exception
A memory leak caused by unclosed resources
Two or more threads permanently blocked, each waiting on a lock the other holds
A thread that runs forever without finishing
questions.explanation: In a deadlock, every involved thread is stuck waiting for a resource held by another thread in the same cycle — none of them can make progress without external intervention.

questions.prompt: Two methods each lock two shared objects, but in opposite order (A then B, versus B then A). What's a standard fix to prevent deadlock?
choices: Remove all synchronization
Add more threads to the pool
Always acquire the locks in the same, consistent global order in every method
Use volatile instead of synchronized
questions.explanation: Deadlock from lock-ordering typically disappears once every code path acquires shared locks in the same fixed order, removing the circular-wait condition.

items.title: ConcurrentModificationException
items.context: Modifying a collection (e.g. calling list.remove()) while iterating over it with a for-each loop or a plain Iterator typically throws ConcurrentModificationException. The fix is to use the Iterator's own remove() method, or a collection designed for concurrent mutation.

questions.prompt: What commonly causes a ConcurrentModificationException?
choices: Sorting a list before iterating it
Structurally modifying a collection directly while iterating over it, outside the iterator's own methods
Iterating over an empty collection
Using a for-each loop on an array
questions.explanation: Most collections' iterators detect structural changes (add/remove) made outside the iterator itself during iteration and fail fast with this exception, rather than risk undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: You need to remove some elements from a list while iterating over it. What avoids ConcurrentModificationException?
choices: Call list.remove(element) directly inside the for-each loop
Use the Iterator's own remove() method, or collect matches first and remove them after the loop
Wrap the loop in a try/catch and ignore the exception
Convert the list to an array first
questions.explanation: Iterator.remove() is specifically designed to mutate the collection safely mid-iteration; alternatively, collect what needs removing during the loop and remove it afterward.

items.title: CompletableFuture
items.context: CompletableFuture extends the older Future with the ability to chain non-blocking callbacks (thenApply, thenCompose, thenCombine) instead of blocking on get(), making it much easier to compose asynchronous operations.

questions.prompt: What can CompletableFuture do that a plain Future cannot?
choices: Chain callbacks to run when the result becomes available, without blocking to poll it
Be cancelled
Run on a background thread at all
Return a value at all
questions.explanation: A plain Future only offers a blocking get(); CompletableFuture lets you attach continuations (thenApply/thenAccept/thenCompose/...) that run automatically once the result is ready.

questions.prompt: Which CompletableFuture method combines the results of two independent futures once both complete?
choices: thenApply
supplyAsync
thenCombine
join
questions.explanation: thenCombine(other, combiner) waits for both CompletableFutures to complete and then applies a function to their two results together.

items.title: Daemon threads
items.context: A daemon thread runs in the background and doesn't keep the JVM alive by itself — once every non-daemon (user) thread has finished, the JVM exits, terminating any remaining daemon threads immediately, without waiting for them to finish.

questions.prompt: What happens to daemon threads once all non-daemon threads in a JVM have finished?
choices: The JVM exits, and daemon threads are terminated abruptly
Nothing changes; the JVM never exits
Daemon threads are promoted to non-daemon threads
The JVM waits for daemon threads to finish too
questions.explanation: The JVM only stays alive while at least one non-daemon thread is running; once those all finish, it exits and any daemon threads are cut off mid-execution.

items.title: Race conditions
items.context: A race condition occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing or interleaving of multiple threads accessing shared state — the outcome can differ from run to run.

questions.prompt: What best defines a race condition?
choices: A deadlock between two threads
Any use of multiple threads
A bug where the program's outcome depends on the unpredictable timing/interleaving of concurrent threads
A program that runs slower under load
questions.explanation: Race conditions arise specifically when shared mutable state is accessed by multiple threads without proper synchronization, making correctness depend on timing that isn't guaranteed.

items.title: ReentrantLock vs synchronized
items.context: ReentrantLock offers everything synchronized does, plus extras: tryLock() with a timeout, interruptible lock acquisition, and an optional fairness policy. The trade-off is that you must explicitly unlock() it yourself, typically in a finally block — synchronized releases its lock automatically even if an exception is thrown.

questions.prompt: What can ReentrantLock do that synchronized cannot?
choices: Guarantee visibility of shared variables
Attempt to acquire the lock with a timeout via tryLock(), and support interruptible waiting
Prevent race conditions
Be reentered by the same thread
questions.explanation: synchronized blocks indefinitely until the lock is available; ReentrantLock adds tryLock(timeout) and lockInterruptibly(), letting a thread give up or be interrupted instead of waiting forever.

questions.prompt: What must you remember to do when using a ReentrantLock that synchronized handles for you automatically?
choices: Explicitly call unlock(), typically in a finally block, or the lock stays held forever if an exception occurs
Manually implement wait()/notify()
Declare the lock as volatile
Nothing extra is required
questions.explanation: Unlike synchronized, which releases its lock automatically on block exit (even via exception), ReentrantLock requires an explicit unlock() — almost always placed in a finally block to guarantee it runs.

items.title: Immutability and thread safety
items.context: An immutable object's state can never change after construction, so multiple threads can freely read it without any synchronization — there's nothing to race over. This is why String and the java.time classes are safe to share across threads with no extra effort.

questions.prompt: Why are immutable objects inherently thread-safe?
choices: They aren't actually thread-safe without explicit synchronization
Because their state can never change after construction, so there is nothing for concurrent threads to race over
Because the JVM automatically synchronizes access to them
Because they are always stored in a special thread-safe memory region
questions.explanation: Thread-safety hazards come from concurrent reads and writes to mutable shared state; if an object can never be modified after it's built, every thread just sees the same fixed state, with no synchronization needed.

items.title: ThreadLocal
items.context: ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own independent copy of a variable, avoiding shared-state synchronization entirely. In a thread-pool environment, forgetting to call remove() on a ThreadLocal can leak memory, since pooled threads are reused indefinitely and keep carrying stale values.

questions.prompt: What does a ThreadLocal variable provide?
choices: A variable that resets to null after every method call
A read-only constant
A variable shared and synchronized across all threads
An independent copy of a variable per thread, isolated from other threads
questions.explanation: Each thread accessing a ThreadLocal sees its own separately stored value — reads and writes from one thread never affect what another thread sees through the same ThreadLocal.

questions.prompt: An application uses a thread pool and stores per-request data in a ThreadLocal, but never calls remove() on it. What risk does this create?
choices: It causes a deadlock
The application will fail to compile
A memory leak: pooled threads are reused indefinitely, so stale values linger and accumulate across requests
No risk, ThreadLocal auto-clears after each request
questions.explanation: Thread-pool threads outlive any single task, so a ThreadLocal value set during one request stays attached to that thread until explicitly removed — across many requests this can leak memory and even leak data between unrelated requests handled by the same pooled thread.

items.title: Semaphore
items.context: A Semaphore controls how many threads may access a resource concurrently, via a fixed number of permits: acquire() takes one (blocking if none are available), release() gives one back. A Semaphore with a single permit behaves like a mutex/lock.

questions.prompt: What does a Semaphore primarily control?
choices: How long a thread pool waits before shutting down
How many threads may concurrently access a resource, via a limited number of permits
Whether a variable is visible across threads
The exact order threads run in
questions.explanation: A Semaphore is initialized with a permit count; acquire() blocks once all permits are taken, and release() returns one — a general way to cap concurrent access to a limited resource (e.g. a connection pool).

questions.prompt: A Semaphore initialized with exactly one permit behaves most like which other construct?
choices: A thread pool
A mutex/lock — only one thread can hold the single permit at a time
An unbounded queue
A CountDownLatch
questions.explanation: With only one permit available, a Semaphore admits exactly one thread at a time, just like a mutual-exclusion lock — this is sometimes called a 'binary semaphore'.

items.title: Happens-before and the Java Memory Model
items.context: The Java Memory Model defines a happens-before relationship: if action A happens-before action B, A's effects (including writes to variables) are guaranteed visible to B. Proper synchronization (synchronized, volatile, thread start/join, ...) establishes happens-before edges; without them, one thread has no guarantee it will ever see another thread's writes.

questions.prompt: What does a happens-before relationship between two actions guarantee?
choices: That both actions run at exactly the same time
That the effects of the earlier action are visible to the later one
That the two actions run on the same thread
Nothing — happens-before is just a naming convention
questions.explanation: happens-before is the Java Memory Model's core guarantee: if properly established (e.g. via synchronized, volatile, or thread join), a later action is guaranteed to see the memory effects of an earlier one — without it, visibility isn't guaranteed even if the write 'already happened' in wall-clock time.

items.title: Producer-consumer with BlockingQueue
items.context: BlockingQueue implementations (like ArrayBlockingQueue and LinkedBlockingQueue) provide put() and take() methods that block automatically when the queue is full or empty, respectively — implementing the producer-consumer pattern without any manual wait()/notify() code.

questions.prompt: What does BlockingQueue's put()/take() pair do that makes it well-suited to the producer-consumer pattern?
choices: They automatically retry failed database writes
They run asynchronously on a separate thread automatically
put() blocks when the queue is full and take() blocks when it's empty, coordinating producers and consumers without manual wait()/notify()
They guarantee FIFO ordering only for single-threaded use
questions.explanation: BlockingQueue handles the coordination that wait()/notify() would otherwise require by hand: producers calling put() pause when there's no room, and consumers calling take() pause when there's nothing to consume, resuming automatically as space or items become available.

items.title: Thread priority
items.context: Thread.setPriority() only hints to the OS scheduler which threads should be favored — it's not a guarantee. Actual scheduling behavior varies by platform and JVM, so priority should never be relied on for correctness.

questions.prompt: Does calling Thread.setPriority(Thread.MAX_PRIORITY) guarantee that thread runs before others?
choices: No, it's only a scheduling hint; actual behavior depends on the OS and JVM
It guarantees the thread never blocks
Yes, but only on Windows
Yes, higher-priority threads always run first
questions.explanation: Thread priority is advisory, not a hard guarantee — the underlying OS scheduler decides how to actually use it, and behavior can differ across platforms, so correctness should never depend on priority alone.

items.title: shutdown() vs shutdownNow()
items.context: ExecutorService.shutdown() stops accepting new tasks but lets already-submitted (running and queued) tasks finish. shutdownNow() instead attempts to stop actively executing tasks immediately (via interruption) and returns the list of tasks that were still waiting in the queue, never started.

questions.prompt: What's the key difference between ExecutorService.shutdown() and shutdownNow()?
choices: They behave identically
shutdown() lets already-submitted tasks finish; shutdownNow() tries to stop running tasks immediately and returns the tasks that never started
shutdownNow() is only for scheduled executors
shutdown() immediately kills all tasks
questions.explanation: shutdown() is the graceful option — no new tasks accepted, but existing work completes; shutdownNow() is more aggressive, attempting to interrupt in-flight tasks right away and handing back whatever was still queued and unstarted.

items.title: Sizing a thread pool
items.context: A common rule of thumb: for CPU-bound tasks, size the pool close to the number of available CPU cores (more threads than cores just adds context-switch overhead). For I/O-bound tasks, a larger pool often helps, since threads spend much of their time blocked waiting on I/O rather than using the CPU.

questions.prompt: For a CPU-bound workload (heavy computation, little waiting), what pool size is generally recommended?
choices: Always exactly 1 thread
As many threads as possible, unbounded
Roughly the number of available CPU cores
Double the number of cores, always
questions.explanation: For purely CPU-bound work, threads beyond the number of cores just compete for the same CPU time via context switching rather than doing more real work in parallel — sizing near the core count is the common starting point.

questions.prompt: Why might an I/O-bound workload benefit from a larger thread pool than a CPU-bound one?
choices: I/O-bound tasks always run faster with fewer threads
There's no difference between I/O-bound and CPU-bound sizing
I/O operations use more CPU than computation
Threads blocked waiting on I/O aren't using the CPU, so more of them can be in flight without CPU contention
questions.explanation: A thread blocked on network or disk I/O isn't consuming CPU, so a larger pool lets more I/O-bound tasks be in progress concurrently without the CPU-contention penalty that oversizing a CPU-bound pool would cause.

items.title: ScheduledExecutorService
items.context: ScheduledExecutorService schedules tasks to run after a delay or repeatedly at a fixed rate/delay — a more capable, thread-pool-based replacement for the older, single-threaded Timer/TimerTask.

questions.prompt: What does ScheduledExecutorService let you do that a plain ExecutorService doesn't?
choices: Run tasks on multiple JVMs at once
Automatically retry failed tasks
Schedule tasks to run after a delay, or repeatedly at a fixed rate/interval
Guarantee tasks never fail
questions.explanation: ScheduledExecutorService adds schedule()/scheduleAtFixedRate()/scheduleWithFixedDelay() for delayed and periodic execution, built on a thread pool — a more robust, concurrent alternative to the legacy single-threaded Timer/TimerTask.

items.title: Future vs CompletableFuture
items.context: A plain Future only supports blocking on get() to retrieve its result (or isDone() polling) — there's no way to attach a callback or combine it with other asynchronous work. CompletableFuture supports both producing and consuming results non-blockingly, and composing multiple async operations together.

questions.prompt: What is a fundamental limitation of a plain Future that CompletableFuture addresses?
choices: Future cannot run on a thread pool
Future offers no way to register a callback or compose it with other async work — you can only block on get()
Future cannot return a value
Future cannot be cancelled
questions.explanation: A plain Future's only way to get a result is a blocking get() call (or polling isDone()); it can't be chained, combined with another Future, or have a callback registered — exactly what CompletableFuture was introduced to solve.

items.title: Unbounded thread pools
items.context: Executors.newCachedThreadPool() creates new threads on demand with no upper bound, reusing idle ones when available. Under sustained heavy load where tasks arrive faster than they finish, this can create an unbounded number of threads and exhaust memory or OS thread limits.

questions.prompt: A service under heavy, sustained load uses Executors.newCachedThreadPool() and starts running out of memory. What's a likely contributing factor?
choices: The JVM ignores thread pools entirely
Cached thread pools don't support Runnable tasks
newCachedThreadPool() has no upper bound on thread count, so it can create huge numbers of threads when tasks arrive faster than they complete
newCachedThreadPool() has a small fixed size that's too small
questions.explanation: Because newCachedThreadPool() will keep spinning up new threads for every task that finds no idle thread available, a sustained flood of slow-to-complete tasks can grow the pool without bound — a bounded pool (like newFixedThreadPool with a sensible queue) avoids this failure mode.

items.title: Locking on an instance vs a class
items.context: A synchronized instance method locks on `this` (the specific object). A synchronized static method locks on the Class object itself, shared by all instances — these are two independent locks, so a thread inside one doesn't block a different thread inside the other.

questions.prompt: Do a synchronized instance method and a synchronized static method on the same class share the same lock?
choices: Yes, always the same lock
No — the instance method locks on `this`, the static method locks on the Class object, so they're independent locks
Only if the class has no constructor
It depends on the JVM vendor
questions.explanation: synchronized instance methods synchronize on the specific object instance (this); synchronized static methods synchronize on the Class object shared by the whole class — two separate monitors, so holding one doesn't block a thread trying to enter the other.

items.title: Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation
items.context: Deadlock: threads are frozen, each waiting on a lock the other holds. Livelock: threads keep actively changing state in response to each other but never make actual progress (like two people repeatedly stepping aside for each other in a hallway). Starvation: a thread is perpetually denied the resources/CPU time it needs, even though the system as a whole is progressing.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes a livelock from a deadlock?
choices: In a livelock, threads keep actively changing state in response to each other without making real progress, rather than being completely frozen as in a deadlock
Livelock only happens with a single thread
Livelock is a synonym for starvation
They are the same thing
questions.explanation: Deadlocked threads are stuck motionless; livelocked threads are very much active — repeatedly reacting to each other's state changes — but never actually complete their work, which can be even trickier to diagnose since the system looks 'busy'.

items.title: Volatile in double-checked locking
items.context: In a double-checked-locking Singleton, the instance field must be declared volatile — without it, instruction reordering can let another thread observe a non-null reference to a not-yet-fully-constructed object, because the reference write and the constructor's field writes aren't guaranteed to be ordered without that volatile guarantee.

questions.prompt: Why must the instance field be `volatile` in a double-checked-locking Singleton implementation?
choices: It's just a style convention with no real effect
Without it, instruction reordering could let another thread see a non-null reference to a partially-constructed object
It prevents the class from being subclassed
volatile makes the constructor run faster
questions.explanation: Without volatile, the JVM/CPU may reorder the write of the reference and the writes that initialize the object's fields, so a second thread could see a non-null (but incompletely initialized) instance — volatile establishes the happens-before ordering needed to prevent that.

items.title: Thread pool rejection policies
items.context: When a ThreadPoolExecutor's queue is full and all its threads are busy, a new submitted task is handled by its RejectedExecutionHandler: AbortPolicy (default, throws RejectedExecutionException), CallerRunsPolicy (runs the task on the calling thread instead, providing backpressure), DiscardPolicy (silently drops it), or DiscardOldestPolicy (drops the oldest queued task to make room).

questions.prompt: By default, what happens when you submit a task to a ThreadPoolExecutor whose queue is full and all threads are busy?
choices: It's automatically retried forever
It silently runs on the main thread
The task waits indefinitely
It throws a RejectedExecutionException (the default AbortPolicy)
questions.explanation: Unless a different RejectedExecutionHandler is configured, ThreadPoolExecutor's default AbortPolicy throws RejectedExecutionException the moment a task can't be queued or run — the other policies (CallerRunsPolicy, DiscardPolicy, DiscardOldestPolicy) offer different ways to handle overload gracefully.

items.title: interrupt() is cooperative
items.context: Calling thread.interrupt() doesn't forcibly stop anything — it sets the thread's interrupt flag, and wakes it (with an InterruptedException) if it's currently blocked in an interruptible call like sleep() or wait(). Code that never checks Thread.interrupted() or calls an interruptible method will simply ignore the interrupt.

questions.prompt: What actually happens when you call thread.interrupt() on a thread that's busy in a tight computational loop with no blocking calls?
choices: It throws an exception on the calling thread
The thread is forcibly terminated immediately
Nothing at all happens, not even the flag is set
Its interrupt flag is set, but the loop keeps running unless the code explicitly checks Thread.interrupted()
questions.explanation: interrupt() is a cooperative signal, not a forced stop: it flips a flag (and wakes the thread early if it's blocked in an interruptible call), but code that never checks that flag or calls an interruptible method will simply run to completion, oblivious to the interrupt.

items.title: Deadlock via inconsistent lock ordering

questions.prompt: What is the likely outcome of running this code?
choices: Deadlock — the threads can hang forever
Always completes quickly
Compile error
Throws IllegalMonitorStateException
questions.explanation: t1 locks A then waits for B while t2 locks B then waits for A — a classic circular wait. If both threads acquire their first lock before either tries for the second, neither can ever proceed: a deadlock. The fix is to always acquire shared locks in the same global order.

items.title: wait() outside synchronized
items.context:
Object lock = new Object();
lock.wait();

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs (outside any synchronized block)?
choices: Compiles but does nothing
Throws InterruptedException
Throws IllegalMonitorStateException
Waits forever
questions.explanation: wait() (and notify()/notifyAll()) may only be called while the current thread holds the object's monitor lock. Calling it outside a synchronized(lock) block throws IllegalMonitorStateException immediately.

items.title: ExecutorService.shutdown() semantics

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Only task A runs; submitting B throws RejectedExecutionException
shutdown() blocks until both tasks finish, then both run
Both tasks A and B run
Only task B runs
questions.explanation: shutdown() stops the pool from accepting new tasks but lets already-submitted tasks finish running. Task A was submitted before shutdown() so it still runs; submitting task B afterward is rejected with RejectedExecutionException. (shutdownNow() additionally tries to interrupt in-flight tasks.)

items.title: Missing volatile on a shared flag

questions.prompt: What is the risk with this code?
choices: None — it always prints "stopped" quickly
Compile error: stop must be final
Throws ConcurrentModificationException
The worker thread may never see the update and spin forever
questions.explanation: stop is a plain field with no volatile, no lock, and no other synchronization. The JIT compiler and CPU caches are free to let the worker thread keep reading a cached copy of flag.stop that never reflects the main thread's write — there's no happens-before edge between the write and the read, so the loop may spin forever in practice. Marking stop volatile fixes it.

items.title: Reentrant synchronized methods

questions.prompt: What happens when outer() is called?
choices: Deadlock — the thread already holds the lock
Prints "inner" normally
Compile error
Throws IllegalMonitorStateException
questions.explanation: Java's intrinsic locks are reentrant: a thread that already holds an object's monitor can enter another synchronized method on the same object without blocking. If they weren't reentrant, this exact pattern — a synchronized method calling another synchronized method on itself — would deadlock every time.

items.title: Exception propagation in CompletableFuture

questions.prompt: What happens when join() is called?
choices: Throws a CompletionException wrapping the RuntimeException
Throws the original RuntimeException("boom") directly
Blocks forever
Returns null silently
questions.explanation: When the supplier passed to supplyAsync() throws, CompletableFuture captures it and wraps it in a CompletionException (join()) or ExecutionException (get()) when you try to retrieve the result. You typically unwrap it with getCause() or handle it via exceptionally()/handle().

items.title: Race condition on a shared counter

questions.prompt: What does this print?
choices: Always exactly 200000
Throws an exception
Some number less than or equal to 200000, usually less — it's not reliably deterministic
Always exactly 100000
questions.explanation: counter[0]++ is read-modify-write, not atomic. When both threads read the same value before either writes it back, one increment is lost. The exact final number varies between runs and JVMs, but it's almost always less than 200,000 — a textbook race condition. Using AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() would make it always exactly 200,000.

items.title: ThreadLocal leaking across pooled tasks

questions.prompt: What does the second submitted task print?
choices: Throws an exception
null — a new ThreadLocal instance is created per task
"request-A" — ThreadLocal is shared across all tasks
"request-A" — because the pool reuses the same worker thread and the value was never cleared
questions.explanation: A ThreadLocal's value is tied to the thread, not the task or the ThreadLocal instance's lifetime. With a single-thread pool, both tasks run on the same physical thread, so the second task sees the value the first task set — unless it's explicitly cleared with ctx.remove(). This is a common source of data leaking between requests in thread-pooled servers.

items.title: try-with-resources close order

questions.prompt: What is the order of output?
choices: body, close A, close B
body, close B, close A
close A, close B, body
close B, close A, body
questions.explanation: try-with-resources closes resources in the reverse order of their declaration — last declared, first closed — similar to unwinding a stack. So b (declared second) is closed before a.

items.title: Double-checked locking without volatile

questions.prompt: What is the bug in this double-checked-locking singleton?
choices: There is no bug, it's correct and thread-safe as written
instance is not declared volatile, so another thread can observe a half-constructed instance
synchronized blocks can't be nested like this — compile error
getInstance() will deadlock on the second call
questions.explanation: Without volatile, the JVM/CPU may reorder the write so that `instance` is visibly non-null before the constructor has fully run. A second thread's first (unsynchronized) null-check can then see a non-null reference to a partially-initialized object. Declaring the field `private static volatile Lazy instance;` establishes the happens-before edge needed to fix it (guaranteed since Java 5).
